element_a.enriched_title: Pronoun and occupation co-occurrence counts in ELMo training corpus
element_a.enriched_content: Aggregate frequency statistics are reported for male (M) and female (F) pronouns in the ELMo training corpus, alongside how often each pronoun co-occurs with stereotypically male-biased versus female-biased occupation terms. The comparisons characterize gender imbalance both in overall entity mention rates (M vs F pronoun totals) and in association patterns between pronouns and occupation stereotypes (M pronouns with M-biased jobs, F pronouns with F-biased jobs). These corpus-level co-occurrence asymmetries motivate later claims that contextual embeddings can encode and propagate gender information unequally across male and female entities.

element_b.caption: Figure 1: Five example images from the imSitu visual semantic role labeling (vSRL) dataset. Each image is paired with a table describing a situation: the verb, cooking, its semantic roles, i.e agent, and noun values filling that role, i.e. woman. In the imSitu training set, $33 \%$ of cooking images have man in the agent role while the rest have woman. After training a Conditional Random Field (CRF), bias is amplified: man fills $16 \%$ of agent roles in cooking images. To reduce this bias amplification our calibration method adjusts weights of CRF potentials associated with biased predictions. After applying our methods, man appears in the agent role of $20 \%$ of cooking images, reducing the bias amplification by $2 5 \%$ , while keeping the CRF vSRL performance unchanged.

element_a.enriched_content: A unit square error-rate space is reduced to a triangular region bounded by the axes and the descending diagonal from (0,1) to (1,0), with a grey shaded subset indicating points satisfying both calibration and an additional constraint. A dashed concave curve runs inside the triangle, acting as a constraint boundary that further limits feasible (FP,FN) combinations. Two operating points, h1 (higher FN, lower FP) and h2 (lower FN, higher FP), are marked, with blue and red line segments from the origin illustrating different trade-offs and how each point relates to the constraint boundaries. The layout highlights that calibration plus the general constraint restricts admissible classifiers to a narrower band, forcing movement along constrained directions rather than arbitrary error-rate improvements.

element_a.enriched_content: Three side-by-side panels compare two demographic groups’ achievable trade-offs between generalized false positive and false negative rates under different fairness constraints. Under “Equal Odds (Trained)” and “Equal Odds (Derived),” each group traces an approximately linear frontier (blue and red lines), with candidate classifiers clustered around x≈0.3–0.5 and y≈0.4–0.6 and diamonds denoting post-processed solutions. Under “Calib. + Equal F.P.” a vertical dashed line near x≈0.45 marks equalized generalized F.P.; the selected group points align in F.P. but remain separated in F.N. (blue around y≈0.45 vs red around y≈0.6), indicating residual disparity and a shift toward higher error for at least one group when adding calibration constraints.

element_a.enriched_content: The formula computes the generalized false-positive rate for a perfectly calibrated classifier within group G_t. It takes the difference between the group-average prediction E[h_t(x)] and the group-average squared prediction E[h_t(x)^2], which captures how much probability mass the classifier assigns without being overly concentrated near 0 or 1. This difference is then normalized by 1−mu_t, adjusting the rate by the group’s negative-class prevalence so the quantity behaves like a false-positive rate. In the paper’s fairness analysis, it provides an explicit closed-form expression for error rates of calibrated classifiers in terms of moments of the score distribution within each group.

element_b.enriched_title: Latent-variable generative sampling of x conditioned on z and s

variables.z: latent code sampled from a prior distribution
variables.θ: model parameters of the conditional distribution

element_b.enriched_content: The equation specifies a two-step generative process: first draw a latent representation z from a chosen prior, then generate an observed sample x from a model distribution conditioned on both z and an additional variable s. element_a.enriched_content: This expression computes an interventional (g-formula) functional for the distribution of the outcome Y under a mixed intervention that sets A=a along some causal paths while forcing A=bar{a} for the mechanism generating L. The integrand factors into the outcome model p(Y|A=a,C,M,L), the conditional model for L under the reference level p(L|A=bar{a},C,M), the mediator model p(M|A=a,C), and the marginal covariate distribution p(C), and then averages over C, M, and L. In the paper’s method, this functional is used to identify and estimate path-specific effects by combining components from different hypothetical interventions within a single estimand.

element_b.enriched_title: Accuracy–fairness efficient frontier curves for sentencing regression models

enriched_metadata.axes: x-axis: Fairness Loss (0 to ~0.07); y-axis: Mean Squared Error (MSE, ~0.90 to ~1.02).

element_b.enriched_content: Four efficient-frontier curves trace the tradeoff between minimizing fairness loss and minimizing prediction error (MSE). As fairness loss increases from 0 toward ~0.07, MSE decreases from about 1.0 down to roughly 0.905–0.91, with the steepest improvement occurring at very small fairness loss. The group-based approaches cluster near very low fairness loss (≈0–0.01) with MSE around 0.91–0.92, while the individual-fairness curves extend across the full fairness-loss range and generally achieve slightly lower MSE at moderate-to-high fairness loss. Overall, relaxing fairness constraints yields diminishing returns in MSE reduction after about 0.03–0.05 fairness loss.

enriched_metadata.axes: x-axis: Fairness Loss (0 to ~0.07); y-axis: Mean Squared Error (MSE, ~0.90 to ~1.02).

node_group.enriched_content: Four efficient-frontier curves trace the tradeoff between minimizing fairness loss and minimizing prediction error (MSE). As fairness loss increases from 0 toward ~0.07, MSE decreases from about 1.0 down to roughly 0.905–0.91, with the steepest improvement occurring at very small fairness loss. The group-based approaches cluster near very low fairness loss (≈0–0.01) with MSE around 0.91–0.92, while the individual-fairness curves extend across the full fairness-loss range and generally achieve slightly lower MSE at moderate-to-high fairness loss. Overall, relaxing fairness constraints yields diminishing returns in MSE reduction after about 0.03–0.05 fairness loss.

element_b.caption: Figure 1: Five example images from the imSitu visual semantic role labeling (vSRL) dataset. Each image is paired with a table describing a situation: the verb, cooking, its semantic roles, i.e agent, and noun values filling that role, i.e. woman. In the imSitu training set, $33 \%$ of cooking images have man in the agent role while the rest have woman. After training a Conditional Random Field (CRF), bias is amplified: man fills $16 \%$ of agent roles in cooking images. To reduce this bias amplification our calibration method adjusts weights of CRF potentials associated with biased predictions. After applying our methods, man appears in the agent role of $20 \%$ of cooking images, reducing the bias amplification by $2 5 \%$ , while keeping the CRF vSRL performance unchanged.

element_a.enriched_content: Ablation over λ compares bias-related summary statistics (μ, σ, β) under fixed vs infinite context settings and reports Penn Treebank perplexity (Ppl.). Among the reported settings, λ=0.5 yields the best perplexity (116.19) and also the lowest fixed-context β (0.14), while λ=0.8 worsens perplexity (121.00) and corresponds to larger infinite-context dispersion (σ=1.57). element_b.caption: Figure 1: Five example images from the imSitu visual semantic role labeling (vSRL) dataset. Each image is paired with a table describing a situation: the verb, cooking, its semantic roles, i.e agent, and noun values filling that role, i.e. woman. In the imSitu training set, $33 \%$ of cooking images have man in the agent role while the rest have woman. After training a Conditional Random Field (CRF), bias is amplified: man fills $16 \%$ of agent roles in cooking images. To reduce this bias amplification our calibration method adjusts weights of CRF potentials associated with biased predictions. After applying our methods, man appears in the agent role of $20 \%$ of cooking images, reducing the bias amplification by $2 5 \%$ , while keeping the CRF vSRL performance unchanged.

element_a.enriched_title: Tanh encoding, softmax attention weights, and pooled representation

variables.E: input matrix of element/sequence representations (e.g., token embeddings or encoder states)
variables.H: nonlinear transformed representations after applying tanh to E
variables.w: trainable weight vector used to score each representation
variables.alpha: softmax-normalized attention weight vector over elements in E/H
variables.r: final pooled/summary representation computed as an attention-weighted combination

element_a.enriched_content: The equation defines an attention-style pooling mechanism to summarize a set or sequence of vectors. First, the input representations E are passed through a tanh nonlinearity to produce H, which can stabilize and enrich features. Then a trainable vector w scores each element via w^T H, and softmax converts these scores into attention weights alpha that sum to one. Finally, r is computed as a tanh-transformed weighted combination of E using alpha, yielding a single vector summary emphasized toward the most relevant elements.

element_b.enriched_content: Two side-by-side panels use an apple-picking cartoon to contrast equality and equity for three groups (blue, purple, yellow) with different starting heights (box platforms). Under “Equality,” the formalization sets p(Ŷ|A=blue)=p(Ŷ|A=purple)=p(Ŷ|A=yellow), aligning predicted positive rates across groups even though the shortest group has less access to apples (outcomes). element_b.enriched_content: As the number of generated analogies increases (0–160), the count of stereotypic analogies rises for the original embedding (“before”) from ~0 up to about 29. variables.VV^T: orthogonal projector onto the subspace spanned by V
variables.A_i: i-th row (or sample) of A used in the row-wise sum
variables.\\widehat{A}: reference/baseline reconstruction of A used for comparison
variables.\\|\\cdot\\|_F: Frobenius norm measuring total squared reconstruction error
variables.\\|\\cdot\\|: Euclidean norm for per-row reconstruction error

node_group.enriched_content: This formula defines a loss as the squared reconstruction error of projecting the data matrix A onto the subspace defined by V (via the projector VVᵀ), minus a baseline squared error using a reference reconstruction Â. The first term measures how well the current subspace explains A, while subtracting \|A-Â\|_F^2 turns it into an excess (relative) error against a fixed benchmark. The equality to a sum over i decomposes the total error into per-row (per-sample) contributions, which is useful for multiplicative-update or MW-style procedures that operate on individual constraints/samples in the fair PCA relaxation.

variables.z^*: optimal slack/offset term added to the constraint expression
variables.\\eta: nonnegative scaling/perturbation parameter applied to the constraint residual
variables.\\epsilon: tolerance parameter controlling allowed constraint violation

element_a.enriched_content: The equation shows how a nonnegative scaled residual inequality implies a lower bound on the underlying (unscaled) linear constraint residual. The term (1+\eta) scales the residual A_i\bar{x} - b_i + z^*, while \epsilon/2 provides a small additive tolerance; together they ensure the residual cannot be too negative. As a result, the method can claim approximate feasibility of the i-th constraint up to an \epsilon/2 violation when using the candidate solution \bar{x} (and offset z^*).

element_a.enriched_title: Deriving an epsilon-feasible linear inequality from a scaled condition

variables.A_i: i-th constraint row/operator applied to the solution
variables.z*: optimal slack/shift term added to the constraint expression

element_a.enriched_content: The expression shows that if a scaled version of the residual (A_i x̄ − b_i + z*) is nonnegative up to an added ε/2 margin, then the unscaled residual must be bounded below by −ε. Here A_i x̄ − b_i measures how much the i-th linear constraint is satisfied or violated, and z* acts as a corrective slack/offset. The result converts a condition involving the factor (1−η) into an explicit ε-feasibility guarantee, which is typically used to argue approximate satisfaction of constraints in the method.

variables.d(·,·): metric distance function between two points
variables.i: a selected/reference point (e.g., a center or facility) in N
variables.i*: an alternative/optimal reference point associated with i or y
variables.x: a point in the set X (e.g., a data/client point)
variables.y: a distinguished point being compared against (e.g., target/client)
variables.r_y: radius parameter associated with y (e.g., ball B(y, r_y))
variables.z: nonnegative auxiliary variable used to optimize the worst-case bound

element_a.enriched_content: The display derives an upper bound on the smaller of two relative-distance ratios, comparing how far x is from i (or i*) relative to how far y is from the same reference point. Using triangle-inequality arguments, the distance from i* to x is bounded by a term involving r_y and the path through i, which converts the second ratio into an expression depending only on r_y and d(i,y). The ratios are then relaxed into a one-parameter worst-case form min(z, 2 + 1/z), and maximizing over z ≥ 0 yields the universal constant bound 1 + √2. In the paper’s method, this establishes a constant-factor guarantee (approximation/competitive ratio) for the case where i lies within the ball around x with radius r_y.

element_a.enriched_content: The expression bounds the best (minimum) of two distance ratios—serving x and y via i versus via i*—by progressively replacing unknown distances using the triangle inequality and the fact that i lies within a ball of radius r_y. variables.i*: reference or optimal point associated with y
variables.x: point in set X used to witness the case
variables.r_y: radius parameter around y (e.g., ball radius B(x,r_y))
variables.z: nonnegative scalar substituting a distance ratio in the maximization

node_group.enriched_content: The expression bounds the best (minimum) of two distance ratios—serving x and y via i versus via i*—by progressively replacing unknown distances using the triangle inequality and the fact that i lies within a ball of radius r_y. This converts the ratio involving d(i*,·) into a function of r_y and d(i,y), yielding a worst-case bound that depends only on a single nonnegative ratio z. Maximizing the resulting min(z, 2+1/z) gives a universal constant 1+√2, which serves as an approximation-factor bound for the paper’s case analysis.

variables.i: index of a data point (or client) under consideration
variables.S: subset of points for which the condition must hold
variables.y: a designated reference point/center used to measure distances from i
variables.d(i,y): distance between point i and reference point y under metric d

element_a.enriched_content: The inequality enforces a separation condition: for every point i in the special set S, the distance from i to the reference point y, scaled by the constant factor (1+√2), must still be strictly smaller than the solution-dependent quantity D_i(X). The left-hand side represents a conservative (inflated) notion of how far i is from y, while D_i(X) acts as a benchmark distance determined by the chosen centers X. In the surrounding clustering argument, this condition is used to ensure that points in S are sufficiently closer to y than to whatever distance scale is induced by X, which supports reasoning about feasible center choices and symmetry among cluster types.

variables.L(theta): objective/loss value produced by the model given parameters theta

element_a.enriched_content: This expression states that training consists of choosing model parameters that make an objective (loss) as small as possible. The loss function L(θ) summarizes how well the model performs (and may include additional terms such as regularization or fairness penalties, depending on the paper). Solving this minimization problem yields the parameter setting used to produce the results that are later compared statistically (e.g., via Mann–Whitney U tests in the accompanying tables).

element_b.enriched_title: Accuracy–fairness efficient frontier curves for sentencing regression models

enriched_metadata.axes: x-axis: Fairness Loss (0 to ~0.07); y-axis: Mean Squared Error (MSE, ~0.90 to ~1.02).

element_b.enriched_content: Four efficient-frontier curves trace the tradeoff between minimizing fairness loss and minimizing prediction error (MSE). As fairness loss increases from 0 toward ~0.07, MSE decreases from about 1.0 down to roughly 0.905–0.91, with the steepest improvement occurring at very small fairness loss. The group-based approaches cluster near very low fairness loss (≈0–0.01) with MSE around 0.91–0.92, while the individual-fairness curves extend across the full fairness-loss range and generally achieve slightly lower MSE at moderate-to-high fairness loss. Overall, relaxing fairness constraints yields diminishing returns in MSE reduction after about 0.03–0.05 fairness loss.

Outputs from both classifiers converge into a single filtering module that screens or selects the resulting examples. The filtered output is then passed to COMeT, indicating a preprocessing step intended to mitigate bias by removing or down-weighting examples based on sentiment and regard signals.

variables.h: candidate classifier from the hypothesis class
variables.c_i^1: cost incurred if example i is predicted as class 1
variables.c_i^0: cost incurred if example i is predicted as class 0

element_a.enriched_content: This objective chooses a classifier \(\hat{h}\) from a hypothesis class \(\mathcal{H}\) that minimizes the total, per-example prediction cost over the training set. For each instance \(X_i\), predicting 1 (i.e., \(h(X_i)=1\)) contributes cost \(c_i^1\), while predicting 0 contributes cost \(c_i^0\); the expression mixes these two costs according to the model’s binary output. In the paper’s method, this serves as the core cost-sensitive learning rule, allowing different examples (and potentially different groups) to impose different penalties for the two possible predictions.

enriched_metadata.axes: X-axis: COMPAS decile score (1–10). Y-axis: observed probability of recidivism (0–1).

element_b.enriched_content: Grouped bars report observed recidivism probability by COMPAS decile for Black (gray) and White (orange) defendants, with 95% confidence-interval error bars. Recidivism rises roughly monotonically with score for both groups, from about 0.2–0.3 at deciles 1–2 to about 0.7–0.85 by deciles 8–10. Within most deciles the Black and White rates are close and their confidence intervals substantially overlap, with Black slightly higher in several bins (e.g., around decile 10: ~0.85 Black vs ~0.70 White). Overall, the pattern indicates similar conditional recidivism rates across races at a given COMPAS score, consistent with approximate calibration/test fairness.

element_a.enriched_title: Uniform error bound on estimated group probabilities

variables.p_{\\boldsymbol{a}}: true probability (or mass) associated with group/index \boldsymbol{a}
variables.\\epsilon: target overall error tolerance used in the analysis
variables.|\\mathcal{A}|: number of groups/indices in the set \mathcal{A}
variables.L: problem-dependent smoothness/Lipschitz constant controlling sensitivity of downstream quantities
variables.\\max[L,1]: stabilizing factor ensuring the denominator is at least 1

element_a.enriched_content: This inequality imposes a per-group accuracy requirement: each estimated group probability must be close to its true value within a small absolute error budget. The allowed error shrinks with the number of groups |\mathcal{A}| (distributing a global tolerance across groups) and with the sensitivity factor \max[L,1] (tighter estimates are needed when subsequent computations are more sensitive). In the paper’s method, such a bound typically supports a guarantee that aggregate quantities—such as Wasserstein-based penalties or barycenter-matching objectives computed across all groups—remain within an overall \epsilon-level error.

element_a.enriched_title: Empirical bound on weighted Wasserstein-1 group-to-barycenter penalty

variables.p_{\\boldsymbol{a}}: true mixture weight (probability mass) of group \boldsymbol{a}
variables.\\hat{p}_{\\boldsymbol{a}}: empirical estimate of the group weight
variables.p_{S_{\\boldsymbol{a}}}: true distribution of model beliefs/scores for group \boldsymbol{a}
variables.p_{\\bar{S}}: true barycenter/aggregate reference distribution over scores
variables.\\hat{p}_{S_{\\boldsymbol{a}}}: empirical distribution of scores for group \boldsymbol{a}
variables.\\epsilon: error/slack term bounding the difference between true and empirical quantities

element_a.enriched_content: The inequality upper-bounds the true expected Wasserstein-1 mismatch between each group’s score distribution and a common reference (the barycenter) by the same mismatch computed from empirical (sampled) distributions, plus a slack term \epsilon. Each term in the sums weights a group’s distributional distance by its group prevalence, so the overall penalty reflects average group-to-barycenter discrepancy. In the paper’s method, minimizing the empirical right-hand side encourages all demographic-group histograms of model beliefs to align with the barycenter, while \epsilon represents the estimation/generalization error from using finite samples.

element_a.enriched_title: Weighted Wasserstein-1 distance bound using estimated reference distribution

variables.p_{\\boldsymbol{a}}: mixture weight or probability mass of group \boldsymbol{a}
variables.S_a: random variable or dataset restricted to group a
variables.p_{S_a}: distribution of S conditioned on group a
variables.\\bar{S}: pooled or reference version of S across groups

element_a.enriched_content: The inequality compares the group-weighted average Wasserstein-1 distance from each group distribution to a true pooled reference distribution versus to an estimated (empirical) pooled reference. Each term p_a\,\mathcal{W}_1(p_{S_a},\cdot) measures how far group a’s distribution is from the chosen reference, and the sum aggregates this discrepancy across groups according to their prevalence p_a. The statement provides a bound showing that using the estimated reference \hat{p}_{\bar{S}} yields an objective at least as large as using the true p_{\bar{S}}, supporting the paper’s argument that the empirical construction corresponds to an upper-bounding (conservative) computation of the same geometric quantity (the shaded area).

variables.\\mathcal{A}: index set of groups (e.g., sensitive attribute values)

element_a.enriched_content: The inequality chain bounds the population-level weighted average Wasserstein-1 distance between each group-conditional distribution and the population barycenter by a corresponding empirical quantity plus a small error term \(\epsilon\). The first step replaces unknown population group weights \(p_{\boldsymbol{a}}\) with empirical weights \(\hat{p}_{\boldsymbol{a}}\) (incurring at most \(\epsilon/2\)), and the next step uses triangle-inequality-style splitting to separate the distance to the empirical barycenter from the estimation error in each group distribution. Overall, it justifies using an empirical Wasserstein barycenter objective/regularizer in the method, while guaranteeing it approximates the population target up to \(\epsilon\).
